Canada’s research and development tax incentive framework—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program and complemented by R&D tax credit regimes across nine provinces and one territory—has undergone its most significant legislative expansion in decades. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal SR&ED regime retroactively expanded for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Key statutory reforms include doubling the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds), widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from 10,000,000–50,000,000 to 15,000,000–75,000,000, extending the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) via a three-year average gross revenue test, and restoring the eligibility of depreciable capital property and equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval Process providing upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks, while Québec overhauled its provincial innovation architecture by abolishing seven legacy tax measures in favour of the consolidated, refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation, and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. In addition, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposed further expanding SR&ED to encompass pre-commercialization regulatory validation studies and intellectual property (IP) protection costs for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026.
Crucial audit corrections integrated throughout this report address four recurring areas of compliance error in practitioner literature:

items: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Rate: The federal overhead proxy rate under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations is strictly 55% of the eligible salary base—not 65% (which expired after 2012) or 60% (which applied only in 2013).

Restoration of Equipment Lease Costs: Contrary to secondary practitioner commentary asserting that equipment leases remain excluded, the CRA’s SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026) and modernized Form T661 instructions confirm that qualifying equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, are once again allowable under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods.

Ontario Tax Credit Rates: The refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) rate is 8% (not the pre-June 2016 rate of 10%), and the non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) rate is 3.5% (not 4.5%).

Statutory Filing Deadlines: The 18-month corporate reporting window under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act is enforced by a statutory bar against extensions under subsection 220(2.2), which neither ministerial discretion nor taxpayer relief provisions under subsection 220(3.1) can override.

body.text: 1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program

The Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is not a discretionary grant scheme; it is a statutory entitlement codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Income Tax Regulations (ITR). When a taxpayer’s activities and expenditures satisfy the statutory definitions and filing deadlines, the Minister of National Revenue is required by law to recognise the resulting tax deductions and investment tax credits.
1.1 The Dual-Mechanism Incentive Structure

The federal SR&ED program operates through a two-part statutory mechanism that separates the income tax deduction of R&D outlays from the calculation of investment tax credits. The first calculation determines the Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool. Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, allowable current and qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada are accumulated in a dedicated tax pool. This provision overrides the general prohibition against deducting capital outlays and removes SR&ED expenditures from ordinary business expense limitations under section 18. Taxpayers may deduct all or any portion of their Section 37 pool balance against net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years.

The second calculation determines the Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Regime. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, taxpayers earn an Investment Tax Credit calculated as a specified percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" for the taxation year. Non-refundable ITCs reduce federal Part I income tax otherwise payable and may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years. Under section 127.1 of the ITA, qualifying corporations, eligible Canadian public corporations, and eligible unincorporated individuals may receive all or a portion of their unused current-year ITCs as an immediate cash refund.

Because "allowable SR&ED expenditures" under section 37 and "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) are governed by distinct statutory rules, the two figures rarely match. For example, the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for overhead and the 25% inclusions for Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) enter the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool to generate ITCs, but never enter the Section 37 deduction pool. Conversely, non-arm's length SR&ED contract payments and purchases of used depreciable SR&ED equipment enter the Section 37 deduction pool, but are excluded from earning ITCs under Section 127.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D incentives in Canada is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. This statutory definition conforms generally to the OECD Frascati Manual and establishes an objective legal standard across all industries. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, SR&ED means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of four eligible categories:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. In corporate tax practice, basic research is the least common category of claimed work and is predominantly conducted within universities and research institutes.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Both basic and applied research involve scientific study through experiment or analysis to generate or discover conceptual scientific knowledge when available scientific knowledge is insufficient.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development is the primary category under which commercial businesses claim SR&ED, as the statutory language explicitly encompasses incremental technological improvements to existing commercial products and manufacturing processes.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Support Work: Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight enumerated activities: (i) engineering, (ii) design, (iii) operations research, (iv) mathematical analysis, (v) computer programming, (vi) data collection, (vii) testing, or (viii) psychological research. Support work does not qualify as SR&ED on its own; it is eligible only where it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

body.text: 1.3 Statutory Exclusions under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity from the definition of SR&ED. Even where these activities are technically complex, expensive, or necessary for a project's commercial rollout, expenditures attributable to paragraphs (e) through (k) cannot be claimed for SR&ED tax incentives:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion (generating business-focused insights, consumer surveys, or sales outputs).
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes.

Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities (which frequently disqualifies commercial data analytics projects that study human or market behaviour rather than resolving computer science or technological uncertainties).

Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (note that if a taxpayer conducts eligible SR&ED while prospecting for minerals, the eligible SR&ED work can be claimed provided the excluded prospecting activity is segregated and left out of the claim).
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes (such as iterating a product’s visual form, surface finish, or proportions without resolving an underlying technological uncertainty).

Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection (gathering datasets, even at scale or with significant logistical difficulty, unless directly supporting and commensurate with the needs of a specific eligible SR&ED experiment under paragraph (d)).

body.text: 1.5 Enacted Reforms under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and Budget 2026 Proposals (November 5, 2026)

Auditing contemporary Canadian SR&ED filings requires distinguishing between two distinct waves of federal policy modernization: the enacted legislative amendments under Bill C-15 and the recently tabled proposals in Federal Budget 2026.
A. Enacted Law: Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3)

First announced in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement, refined in draft legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, tabled in the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget (where Department of Finance Table 1 projected a five-year fiscal impact of $293 million from 2025–2026 to 2029–2030), and enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, four foundational statutory amendments are now in force for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), alongside a fifth, administrative reform implemented by the CRA:

items: Doubling of the Enhanced Expenditure Limit: The maximum annual expenditure ceiling eligible for the enhanced 35% federal ITC doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000.

Expansion of the Taxable Capital Phase-Out Corridor: For Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada at which the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to phase out increased from $10,000,000 to $15,000,000, and the upper threshold at which the enhanced limit reaches nil increased from $50,000,000 to $75,000,000.

Extension of the 35% Refundable Credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): Canadian-resident public corporations not controlled by non-residents now have access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, subject to a straight-line phase-out based on three-year average gross revenue between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Qualifying CCPCs may also elect to use this gross revenue phase-out formula in lieu of the taxable capital test.

Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Equipment Leases: Reversing the 2012 Federal Budget repeal (which had eliminated capital and lease eligibility effective January 1, 2014), Bill C-15 restored both the Section 37 deduction and Section 127 ITC eligibility for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024 (including both All-or-Substantially-All capital property and First/Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment), as well as qualifying equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024.

Launch of Elective Pre-Claim Approval (April 1, 2026): As an administrative measure announced in Budget 2025 rather than a Bill C-15 amendment, the CRA operationalized an optional pre-claim approval mechanism via My Business Account and Form T1322, delivering upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks.

body.text: B. Proposed Measures: Federal Budget 2026 (Tabled November 5, 2026)

On November 5, 2026, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue tabled Federal Budget 2026, proposing a second wave of SR&ED modernization aimed at bridging Canada’s commercialization gap and protecting domestic intellectual property. In the Budget 2026 documents, the federal government estimates that these proposed measures will provide $930 million in additional support over five years and $235 million annually thereafter, applying to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (making calendar-year 2027 the earliest applicable year for December 31 year-end corporations).

The first proposed expansion covers Pre-Commercialization Regulatory and Certification Work, bringing into the SR&ED regime certain tests, technological validations, and studies required to satisfy regulatory requirements for initial approval or commercialization certification of a new or improved product or process (particularly relevant to pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medical devices, and advanced manufacturing), provided the validation work directly relates to an otherwise qualifying SR&ED project. Standard expense categories (wages, materials, contracts, overhead, and machinery or equipment) incurred in these validation studies would qualify. The second proposed expansion covers Intellectual Property (IP) Protection Costs incurred during the commercialization process to register and maintain IP developed in a qualifying SR&ED project—specifically encompassing patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. Under the proposal, official filing and maintenance fees paid to foreign IP offices would qualify, whereas supporting professional work (such as preparing and drafting an application) would qualify only if performed in Canada. IP enforcement and litigation costs remain excluded, and ITC recapture rules would apply if the resulting IP is subsequently disposed of. Because these Budget 2026 measures are legislative proposals rather than enacted law as of November 2026, claimants cannot rely on them for prior taxation years.
2. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Phase-Out Mechanics, Refundability, and Carryovers
2.1 Basic (15%) versus Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Rates

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the basic federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rate—referred to in the statute as the "specified percentage"—is 15% of a taxpayer’s SR&ED qualified expenditure pool. This 15% basic rate applies to foreign-controlled corporations and non-qualifying public corporations, to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on qualified expenditures that exceed their annual expenditure limit for the taxation year, to sole proprietorships (unincorporated individuals) and beneficiaries of trusts, and to partnerships (where the ITC is calculated at the partnership level at 15% under subsection 127(8) and allocated to eligible active partners).

Under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, qualifying CCPCs and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations earn an additional 20% enhancement on top of the 15% basic rate, resulting in an enhanced federal ITC rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit.
2.2 The $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

Under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, as amended by Bill C-15, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is $6,000,000 (doubled from the $3,000,000 limit that applied to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). At the 35% enhanced rate, a $6,000,000 expenditure limit generates up to $2,100,000 in federal ITCs per year, compared to $1,050,000 under the former $3,000,000 ceiling.

Under subsection 127(10.3) of the ITA, associated corporations must share a single $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit across the entire associated corporate group using prescribed Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). If associated corporations fail to file Schedule 49, the CRA sets the expenditure limit to nil. Furthermore, the $6,000,000 limit is reduced proportionately for short taxation years (fewer than 365 days) and is subject to specific anti-multiplication rules where a corporation has multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC.
A. Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula for CCPCs

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC’s $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit begins to decrease on a straight-line basis when its taxable capital employed in Canada (combined across all associated corporations in the immediately preceding taxation year) reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000. For a full 365-day taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, the CCPC Expenditure Limit under the taxable capital method is determined by the linear reduction formula:

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $15,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Under this formula, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit is reduced by $1. By contrast, for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the legacy formula phased out the $3,000,000 limit between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital:

Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $10,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000.
B. Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and Electing CCPCs

Bill C-15 introduced the definition of an "eligible Canadian public corporation" (ECPC) in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, a corporation must be a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange, be resident in Canada, and not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by non-resident persons (even if all shares owned by non-residents were instead owned by a single hypothetical person).

To determine the expenditure limit for an ECPC, Bill C-15 established a Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Test. Under this rule, an ECPC’s $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit begins to decrease on a straight-line basis when its average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (as reflected in its financial statements, or consolidated financial statements for a corporate group, with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales of goods or services so the group reflects a single economic entity) exceeds $15,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000:

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if three-year average annual revenue is ≤ $15,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000.

Crucially, under Bill C-15, a CCPC (or associated group of CCPCs) may also elect on a prescribed form to calculate its Expenditure Limit using this three-year average gross revenue formula in place of the taxable capital method. This election benefits capital-intensive startups that have raised over $15,000,000 in balance-sheet capital but have under $15,000,000 in three-year average revenue.
2.3 Refundability Rules and the Qualifying Income Limit (QIL)

Under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, the cash refundability of earned SR&ED ITCs depends on four variables: the legal classification of the claimant, whether the expenditure is within or above the corporation’s Expenditure Limit, whether the expenditure is of a current nature or a capital nature, and whether a CCPC meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" or an "excluded corporation" under subsection 127.1(2).

For both CCPCs (other than excluded corporations) and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC on qualified expenditures up to their $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit, current expenditures are 100% refundable, yielding an immediate cash refund of 35 cents per dollar of qualified current expenditure. Conversely, ITCs earned at the 35% rate on restored depreciable capital expenditures (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) are 40% refundable up to the Expenditure Limit, yielding a direct cash refund of 14 cents per dollar (35% × 40% = 14%) of qualified capital expenditure, with the remaining 60% of the ITC (21% of the capital cost) retained as a non-refundable ITC to offset Part I tax or carry back or forward.

While non-excluded CCPCs and ECPCs receive 100% refundability on current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures) up to their Expenditure Limit, refundability on expenditures above the Expenditure Limit (which earn the 15% basic ITC) and for "excluded corporations" turns on subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA. A Qualifying Corporation is defined in subsection 127.1(2) as a corporation that is a CCPC throughout the taxation year (and not an excluded corporation) whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year—combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year—does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit (QIL). A Qualifying Corporation receives a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on both current and capital expenditures over its Expenditure Limit (an effective 6.0% cash refund plus 9.0% non-refundable ITC).

(For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the denominator in the QIL formula was $40,000,000 and measured taxable capital exceeding $10,000,000 up to $50,000,000).

An Excluded Corporation (a Qualifying Corporation that is controlled by or related to tax-exempt entities or Crown corporations) still earns the 35% enhanced ITC up to the Expenditure Limit, but its refundability on current expenditures up to the limit is reduced from 100% to 40%, matching its 40% refundability on capital expenditures and over-limit expenditures. body.text: 2.5 Special Structural Rules for Partnerships and Joint Ventures

Taxpayers structuring collaborative R&D through partnerships must navigate restrictive statutory rules under section 96 and subsections 127(8) to 127(8.31) of the Income Tax Act, as set out in the CRA’s SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy. Because a partnership is not a "person" or "taxpayer" under subsection 248(1), it cannot claim ITCs directly. However, its net income and SR&ED ITCs are calculated at the partnership level as if it were a separate person under paragraph 96(1)(a). Because the calculation is performed at the partnership level rather than the partner level, all partnership SR&ED ITCs are calculated at the fixed 15% basic rate, even if the partners receiving the allocation are qualifying CCPCs. Furthermore, only partners that are qualifying corporations, individuals, or certain trusts may receive a 40% refund of their allocated partnership ITC; if a partner is a corporation other than a qualifying corporation, the allocated 15% ITC is completely non-refundable.

Under paragraph 127(8)(b) and subsection 127(8.1) of the ITA, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of a partnership. Subsection 248(1) defines a "specified member" as any partner who is a limited partner (under partnership law or subsection 96(2.4)) at any time during the fiscal period, or any general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership’s business activities (other than financing) or carrying on a similar business during the year. Under subsections 127(8.3) and 127(8.31), unallocated ITCs that cannot be allocated to specified members may be reallocated to active general partners (non-specified members) based on what is reasonable in the circumstances considering their investment.

In addition, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) of the ITA, the entire amount in a partnership's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures must be deducted in calculating partnership net income in the year the expenditures are incurred; a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance to future years. Under subsection 127(12.1), any ITC allocated from the partnership to its partners reduces the partnership's Section 37 pool in the subsequent fiscal period (and any partnership ITC recapture excess added to a partner's Part I tax increases the partnership's pool in the subsequent year under paragraph 37(1)(c.3)). A partner cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes, so any salary or wages paid to a partner are treated as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as SR&ED wages. Finally, because a partnership is not a taxpayer, it cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under a non-arm's length contract via Form T1146 under subsection 127(13). By contrast, participants in an unincorporated joint venture file their own separate SR&ED claims directly on their respective corporate tax returns.
2.6 Carryback, Carryforward, and the 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime

Under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127.1(3) of the ITA, a claimant must first apply current-year ITCs to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable for the taxation year. Any remaining ITC eligible for a cash refund under section 127.1 is then refunded and deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax under subsection 127.1(3), reducing the ITC available for carryback or carryforward. Any unapplied, non-refundable ITC balance may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (to reduce prior-year Part I tax to nil, up to the lesser of the unapplied current-year ITC or the prior year's net Part I tax payable) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years under subsection 127(9). Both unused ITCs and undeducted Section 37 pool balances (under subsection 37(6.1)) are subject to carryforward and carryback restrictions following an acquisition of control (loss restriction event).

To prevent taxpayers from claiming SR&ED tax credits on physical assets or materials and subsequently selling them or converting them to commercial use without tax adjustment, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA enforce a 20-year ITC recapture window (detailed in the CRA’s Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy). Recapture is triggered if, within 20 taxation years of earning the ITC, the taxpayer disposes of or converts to commercial use: (1) depreciable SR&ED capital property claimed under paragraph 37(1)(b) (acquired after December 15, 2024, or prior to 2014); (2) First-Term or Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE); or (3) property incorporating "materials transformed" in SR&ED (including custom products, commercial assets, experimental production output, or prototypes sold for proceeds equal to or exceeding 10% of their construction cost).

When recapture applies, the claimant must add to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or commercial conversion an amount based on the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property and the ITC rate applied to the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon commercial conversion or non-arm's length transfer). Under subsection 127(32), if the claimant manufactured a component or inventory batch in-house, the "cost of property acquired" subject to recapture includes only the laid-down cost of materials purchased from suppliers, and does not trigger recapture on the in-house SR&ED labour or overhead used to manufacture the item. Conversely, if the component was purchased under contract from an arm's-length supplier, the entire contract purchase cost of the property (including the supplier's manufacturing cost and profit element) is subject to recapture. However, if an SR&ED contract generates purely intellectual property (IP) whose rights vest in the payer, selling or licensing that IP does not trigger ITC recapture under subsection 127(27) (though Federal Budget 2026 proposes specific recapture rules for the newly proposed IP registration expense category starting on or after November 5, 2026). Any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax payable is simultaneously added back to the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Restoration of Capital and Lease Costs
3.1 Traditional Method versus Proxy Method Election

Every SR&ED claimant must elect on a year-by-year basis in Part 1 of Form T661 whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, if a claimant does not explicitly elect the Proxy Method on Form T661 when first filing the claim for the taxation year, the Traditional Method applies automatically. Once Form T661 is filed for a given taxation year, the selected method is irrevocable for that taxation year, although the taxpayer may switch methods in any subsequent taxation year.
The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Rate is 55%

A frequent technical error in practitioner R&D literature (and a historical artifact in older text of Guide T4088 Line 820 prior to post-2013 rate adjustments) is the claim that the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is 65% of the salary base. Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA’s Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the statutory PPA rate was 65% up to 2012, decreased to 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% of the eligible salary base since January 1, 2014 (including all 2025 and 2026 taxation years).

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically track or allocate overhead and indirect support expenditures to SR&ED. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount—equal to 55% of the salary base (the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, subject to exclusions and specified employee caps) in Part 5 of Form T661 and enters this amount on Line 502 in Part 4 to earn federal and provincial ITCs. The PPA is a purely notional figure: it cannot be added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents (office supplies, utilities, clerical and administrative support wages, general-purpose office equipment or furniture, and routine maintenance) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is subject to an Overall Cap calculated by the formula A − B − C, ensuring that the notional proxy amount cannot exceed total deductible business expenses for the year (A) minus the Section 37 SR&ED deduction claimed (B, per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1) and specified non-overhead deductions (C, such as Capital Cost Allowance, building rent, and interest).

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR, overhead and other expenditures claimed under the Traditional Method must satisfy two cumulative legal tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (excluding any indirect portion), demonstrating a direct linkage—with no intervening step or intermediary—to specific SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or machinery and equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED (or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED under Regulation 2900(3)) not occurred.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employee Caps, Unpaid Wages, and Foreign Work

Under subsection 248(1) and section 5 of the Income Tax Act (and the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, updated January 28, 2025), eligible "salary or wages" include gross T4 employment income, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, bonuses, commissions, honorariums, and actual cash outlays for taxable benefits under section 6 (or non-cash taxable benefits if they represent a reasonable estimate of actual employer cash outlays, exclude GST/HST or PST where input tax credits are claimed, and are not deducted elsewhere as a business expense). Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages exclude the employer’s share of payroll-related benefits (such as employer CPP/QPP, EI, or EHT contributions, which are covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method or claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), extended vacation or sick leave, stock option benefits, retiring allowances, unpaid wages under subsection 78(4), and dividends paid to shareholders.

Under the Proxy Method, only the salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED (hands-on work, plus certain tasks performed by non-specialized employees supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications, and technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects) can be claimed directly. Whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED is determined by the nature of the tasks performed, not the employee's job title. Under the CRA’s administrative 100% Rule, an employee who spends "all or substantially all" (90% or more) of their total employment time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is considered to spend 100% of their time on SR&ED.
A. Specified Employees: The Three Statutory Restrictions

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the corporation—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation (including shares owned by any person with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length, such as a spouse, sibling, or parent)—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions:

items: Total Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (ITA Subsection 37(9)): While bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to regular (non-specified) employees can be included in Section 37 SR&ED wages on Line 300 (though subtracted from the Proxy Salary Base on Line 812), subsection 37(9) completely excludes all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee from SR&ED expenditures.

The 5 × YMPE Section 37 Deductible Salary Cap (ITA Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum amount of directly engaged SR&ED salary or wages (Line 305) that can be claimed for a single specified employee in a taxation year is limited under subsection 37(9.1) to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year the individual was a specified employee: Maximum Specified Employee SR&ED Salary or Wages = 5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year the individual was a specified employee ÷ 365) Under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.5) of the ITA, if an individual is a specified employee of two or more associated corporations, the single 5 × YMPE ceiling is shared across the group and must be allocated among the associated corporations using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development — SR&ED). If associated corporations fail to file Form T1174, the specified employee's salary or wages are deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED across all of them.

The 2.5 × YMPE and 75% Proxy Salary Base Cap (ITR Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8)): When calculating the Salary Base in Part 5 of Form T661 (Boxes 850 to 860) to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount, a specified employee’s eligible proxy salary base is restricted to the lesser of:

Box 856: The specified employee’s total salary or wages for the year (100% of SR&ED and non-SR&ED base salary in Box 852, excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior-year unpaid wages) multiplied by the actual percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Box 854, capped at a maximum of 75%; and

Box 858: 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed: Box 858 = 2.5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year the individual was employed ÷ 365) Under subsection 2900(8) of the ITR, this 2.5 × YMPE proxy base ceiling is also shared across associated corporations.

B. The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration and Unpaid Expenditure Rules

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, if employee salary or wages incurred in a taxation year remain unpaid 180 days after the end of that taxation year (with a payment made on the 180th day accepted as timely by the CRA), the unpaid remuneration is deemed not to have been incurred in that year. Instead, it must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year incurred and is deemed incurred only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (claimed on Line 310). Crucially, under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, prior-year unpaid wages claimed when paid on Line 310 (as well as reasonable vacation or holiday pay and salary deferral arrangements that remain unpaid after 180 days) are excluded from the Proxy Salary Base, meaning failure to pay SR&ED wages within 180 days of year-end forfeits the 55% PPA overhead credit on those wages.

Similarly, under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, current expenditures other than salary or wages (such as materials or arm's-length contractor invoices) incurred in a taxation year but unpaid 180 days after year-end must be deducted from Section 127 qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661. For an unpaid arm's-length SR&ED contract, the 20% reduction is applied first, and the remaining 80% is deducted on Line 520 and added back to qualified expenditures in the subsequent taxation year when paid. If an unpaid amount is not identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline for the year incurred, it can never be included in qualified expenditures even when paid later.
C. Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (The 10% Limit)

While subsection 37(2) of the ITA restricts foreign R&D generally to an ordinary current income deduction with zero ITCs, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA allow a claimant to include "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees) if five cumulative statutory conditions are met:

items: The work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (not performed by a contractor);
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred;
The work was related to a business of the claimant;
The work outside Canada was an integral part of, and solely in support of, the SR&ED work carried on inside Canada; and
The salary or wages paid were not subject to an income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: Under subsection 37(1.5), the maximum allowable claim for permissible foreign SR&ED wages is the lesser of the eligible foreign wages incurred (Amount A) and 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED carried on inside Canada (Amount B, calculated as 10% of Line 306 on Form T661). Permissible foreign wages within this 10% limit are deemed to be expenditures made in Canada, making them eligible for both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 ITCs.
3.3 Materials Consumed versus Materials Transformed, Prototypes, and Pilot Plants

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA, and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR (detailed in the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy, updated March 27, 2026), a claimant under either the Traditional or Proxy Method may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

To constitute "materials for SR&ED", items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) raw materials, substances, or other items that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED. Items that do not compose the body of the experimental object—such as broken or used lab glassware (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas, propane), CDs/DVDs, and used engine lubricants—do not qualify as materials for SR&ED (they are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method or claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method). By contrast, chemical reagents tested on wood, seeds, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, fertilizers or pesticides applied to experimental field test plots, and metal parts subjected to third-party galvanization for SR&ED testing qualify as materials (with the service cost of galvanization forming part of the laid-down cost of the metal). Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, and their eligible laid-down cost includes invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition costs, and storage costs (or, for internally manufactured inventory used in SR&ED, laid-down material cost plus direct manufacturing labour and allocable production overhead). Under subsection 127(11.6), materials purchased from a non-arm's length supplier are restricted for ITC purposes to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length supplier, excluding profit. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED, not when purchased or placed in inventory.

Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, broken down into small pieces, or rendered virtually valueless (having a residual value of less than 10% of their original cost) as a result of the SR&ED. Materials consumed are not subject to ITC recapture unless subsequent proceeds (such as insurance proceeds) exceed 10% of their cost. Materials transformed (Line 325) are raw materials, substances, or component parts that are altered or incorporated during SR&ED into a prototype, custom product, experimental production batch, or commercial asset that retains value. Transformed materials are subject to the 20-year ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (36) if the resulting asset or product is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.

Under the CRA’s SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, the tax treatment of prototypes, pilot plants, commercial plants, and custom products follows strict delineation rules. A prototype is an original trial model possessing the essential characteristics of an intended product, constructed within a systematic investigation to test a hypothesis. Labour and materials used to design, construct, and test a prototype qualify as current SR&ED expenditures. If a prototype is sold for nominal scrap proceeds (less than 10% of its construction cost), the proceeds are included in income and ITC recapture does not apply; if proceeds equal or exceed 10%, ITC recapture applies. Duplicate copies of a prototype constructed solely for experimental testing qualify as materials when consumed or transformed upon completion of testing, whereas copies built for commercial inventory are ineligible. A pilot plant is a non-commercial scale production facility developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED during its useful life (never used for commercial production, sales promotion, or temporary/permanent conversion to commercial operations), for which operating labour and materials consumed or transformed qualify. When SR&ED occurs during the development of a commercial plant, custom product, or commercial asset, claimants must segregate eligible SR&ED work from routine engineering; SR&ED on a specific component does not make the entire asset eligible unless the SR&ED work requires redesigning closely associated components.
3.4 Subcontractors (Arm's-Length versus Non-Arm's-Length) and Third-Party Payments
A. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340 — The 80% ITC Rule)

Under the CRA’s Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy), when a claimant contracts an arm's-length "taxable supplier" to perform SR&ED (or paragraph 248(1)(d) support work that is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the payer’s Canadian SR&ED) on the claimant's behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the payer's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01). However, under paragraph (g) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II), only 80% of the arm's-length contract expenditure is included as a qualified expenditure to earn ITCs. Following Bill C-15, contract expenditures and third-party payments incurred after December 15, 2024, are no longer reduced under the former subsection 37(14) "look-through rule" for capital expenditures incurred by the contractor after December 15, 2024.

To prevent duplication of ITCs, the contractor performing the work must reduce its own qualified SR&ED expenditures by the "contract payment" receivable under subsection 127(18). If an arm's-length contractor is hired to perform only paragraph (d) support work, the contractor cannot claim SR&ED in its own right because support work alone does not meet subsection 248(1), whereas the payer can claim the contract cost. Contract payments for SR&ED work performed outside Canada are not allowable under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and earn 0% ITCs, though they may be deducted against current income under subsection 37(2).
B. Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345 and Form T1146)

Where a claimant (payer) contracts with a non-arm's-length performer (under section 251 of the ITA), the payer's contract expenditures are deductible in the payer's Section 37 pool on Line 345, but under paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), they are not qualified expenditures for ITC purposes (0% ITC for the payer). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own SR&ED expenditures and earns the ITC directly (as payments from a NAL party are not "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) and do not reduce the performer's qualified expenditures). Under subsection 127(13) of the ITA, the NAL performer may transfer all or part of its qualified SR&ED expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the NAL payer by filing prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), reported on Line 508 for the transferee and Line 540 for the transferor on Form T661. Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24) of the ITA, a claimant cannot circumvent the NAL rules by interposing an arm's-length party between the payer and a NAL performer.
C. Third-Party Payments (Line 370 and Form T1263)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and 37(1)(a)(ii) of the ITA (and the CRA’s Third-Party Payments Policy), a claimant may claim payments made to five types of research entities (reported on Line 370 of Form T661 with prescribed Form T1263): Entity A (a Canadian-resident corporation performing basic or applied research whose primary purpose is to use the results in conjunction with the claimant's own SR&ED), Entity B (an approved association), Entity C (an approved university, college, or research institute), Entity D (a tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation under paragraph 149(1)(j)), or Entity E (an approved granting council funding Entities B, C, or D). Like arm's-length contracts, 100% of an eligible third-party payment enters the Section 37 pool and 80% enters Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITCs. Unlike contracts, third-party payment research is controlled by the performer, rights are non-exclusive, and the claimant must be entitled to exploit the results in its business (such as holding a licence to a resulting patent or receiving preferential pre-publication access to findings before they enter the public domain).
3.5 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of capital property and equipment lease expenditures for property acquired or lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. In May and June 2026, the CRA published three updated administrative policies governing these restored rules: the SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026). (While one practitioner blog stated that equipment leases were not restored, official CRA policy documents confirm that equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are allowable under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods.)
A. All or Substantially All (ASA) Depreciable Capital Property (Line 390)

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) (Traditional Method) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) (Proxy Method) of the ITA, an expenditure made to acquire depreciable property (within the meaning of subsection 13(21) of the ITA, owned by the claimant or deemed acquired via a joint lessor-lessee election under section 16.1 of the ITA) after December 15, 2024 (and "available for use" under subsection 37(1.2) after December 15, 2024) qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either:

items: That the property would be used during All or Substantially All (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada; or
That All or Substantially All (90% or more) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

body.text: Qualifying ASA capital expenditures are claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 and enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Any deduction claimed from the Section 37 pool for capital property is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) in a separate prescribed class (subject to CCA recapture on Line 440 and 20-year ITC recapture under subsection 127(27)), and the property must not be included on regular Schedule T2SCH8. While used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, meeting the ASA test can be claimed on Line 390 to enter the Section 37 deduction pool, used property is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations and is excluded from earning Section 127 ITCs (unless refurbished to a new state). Non-depreciable property (land, inventory, goodwill) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (except special-purpose buildings prescribed under Regulation 2903) are excluded.
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504: First-Term and Second-Term 25% Rules)

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and the CRA’s SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 if it is: (1) new property; (2) used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the statutory period; (3) not General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF); and (4) not "Prescribed Depreciable Property" (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the ITR (which excludes property intended at acquisition to be used in assembling or commissioning a commercial plant or intended to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes over its expected useful life).
SUE treatment is identical under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods:

items: First-Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): If the equipment is used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED during the First Period (from the date acquired and available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time), 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21 and adjusted for non-arm's length costs under subsection 127(11.6)) is included as a qualified expenditure on Line 504.

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): If the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and is used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED during the Second Period (from the date acquired and available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time), a second 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost is included as a qualified expenditure on Line 504.

body.text: Thus, SUE earns ITCs on up to 50% of its capital cost across two periods. The capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool; instead, the claimant depreciates SUE via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 (with UCC reduced in the subsequent year by SUE ITCs claimed or refunded).
C. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Incurred After December 15, 2024)
Under the CRA’s SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are claimed according to the method elected:

items: Under the Traditional Method: If leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I). If leased equipment is used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the proportional percentage of the lease cost used for SR&ED may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR, provided it is directly related and incremental to SR&ED. Lease costs for land or structures (such as a bridge or dam) incurred after December 15, 2024, are also allowable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable.

Under the Proxy Method: If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I). If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost may be claimed under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI). If leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% can be claimed under the Proxy Method. Bandwidth is allowable as a lease of equipment under the Proxy Method, whereas lease of land and GPOEF are excluded under the Proxy Method.

Universal Building Rent Exclusion: Under paragraph 37(8)(d)(ii) and subparagraph 37(8)(e)(i) of the ITA, rent or lease expenditures for the use or right to use a building are excluded under both methods (unless prescribed as a special-purpose building under Regulation 2903).

body.text: 3.6 Cloud Computing, Software Subscriptions, Overhead Nuances, and Prescribed Exclusions

Cloud computing subscriptions and CAD or software licences are ordinary business deductions under paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA. Under the Proxy Method, they are covered inside the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately (unless qualifying as a dedicated post-December 15, 2024 equipment or bandwidth lease under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) or (VI)), whereas under the Traditional Method, they can be claimed on Line 360 only if proven directly related and incremental to SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR. Outright purchases of computers, GPUs, and software bought after December 15, 2024, and used ≥90% for SR&ED qualify as restored capital property.

Under the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, Traditional Method claimants may claim on Line 360 incremental costs for travel and lodging in Canada to perform testing at a customer location, training in Canada, clinical study volunteer fees, health and safety expenses, and moving expenses to relocate SR&ED employees or selected candidates within Canada. Conversely, headhunter fees, hiring advertisements, selection travel, immigration or visa costs, fixed-cost maintenance contracts, and post-project waste disposal fail the incremental test and are excluded. Furthermore, section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations designates general administration or management (Subparagraph 2902(a)(i)), legal or accounting fees (Clause 2902(a)(i)(B)), interest and financing costs (Clause 2902(a)(i)(C)), conventions or conferences (Clause 2902(a)(i)(F)), and fees for preparing SR&ED claims as prescribed expenditures that never earn ITCs.
3.7 Government and Non-Government Assistance (Subsections 127(18)–(20) and Form T1145)

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act (detailed in the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy), a claimant must reduce both its Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and its Section 127 qualified expenditure pool by any government assistance (such as NRC IRAP grants, conditionally repayable contributions, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its filing due date for the taxation year. Non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance among themselves using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20). When assistance or a contract payment is subsequently repaid, the repayment is added back to the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earns an ITC in the year repaid under paragraphs (e.1)/(e.2) of subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.7) at the exact ITC rate that would have been earned in the year the assistance originally reduced the claim.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits. All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—except Québec’s CO-17 regime (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta’s AT1 regime (administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance)—are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency via T2 corporate schedules and are harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED. Three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.
4.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario operates three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered by the CRA. Claimants must ensure working papers apply the post-May 31, 2016 statutory rates of 8% for the OITC and 3.5% for the ORDTC, rather than the legacy 10% and 4.5% rates:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — 8% Refundable): A fully refundable 8% tax credit available to qualifying corporations on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (maximum annual refund of $240,000). The $3,000,000 OITC limit phases out when prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000, or when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000. Claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — 3.5% Non-Refundable): A non-refundable 3.5% tax credit (section 39 of the Taxation Act, 2007) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (net of OITC and OBRITC) with no expenditure cap, carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years. As confirmed in the 2026 Ontario Fall Statement, the ORDTC includes the impact of the federal restoration of capital expenditures acquired on or after December 16, 2024. Claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508, along with transitional schedules T2SCH506 and T2SCH507 where applicable).

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — 20% Refundable): A fully refundable 20% tax credit (section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007) for qualified expenditures incurred under eligible research contracts with approved Ontario research institutes (universities, colleges, hospital research institutes), subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap. Claimed on Schedule 568 (T2SCH568) and Schedule 569 (T2SCH569).

body.text: 4.2 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul and Legacy Transition Rules
In its March 25, 2025 Budget (Budget 2025–2026), the Gouvernement du Québec introduced a comprehensive reform of its provincial R&D tax assistance system, administered by Revenu Québec.
A. The New Regime: Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation, and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)

Effective for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D, l'innovation et la précommercialisation) replaces and eliminates seven legacy Québec tax measures: (1) the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (RD-1029.7-V); (2) the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium (RD-1029.8.6-V); (3) the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (RD-1029.8.16.1-V); (4) the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (RD-1029.8.9.03-V, with transitional relief for cumulative balances until December 31, 2029); (5) the tax credit for technological adaptation services; (6) the industrial design component of the design tax credits; and (7) the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

Under the CRIC, every qualified corporation carrying on business with an establishment in Québec—regardless of its asset size (eliminating the legacy $50,000,000 to $75,000,000 asset phase-out)—earns a fully refundable 30% tax credit on up to $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold (associated corporations allocate the $1,000,000 limit using Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and a fully refundable 20% basic rate on qualified expenditures above $1,000,000. Corporations claiming the CRIC as members of a partnership earn only the 20% base rate, and unincorporated individuals cannot claim the CRIC.

The CRIC covers both R&D activities (harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition and reviewed scientifically by the CRA) and eligible pre-commercialization activities performed in Québec as a continuation of Québec R&D. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include: (a) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements to obtain initial approval or certification for commercialization, and (b) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials. Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of eligible employee salaries and wages, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to eligible Québec public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs for new depreciable property used almost exclusively in Québec R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and excluding property under a Large Investment Project tax holiday).

For each taxation year, qualified expenditures must exceed an Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold (calculated as the basic personal amount of the applicable Québec personal income tax system for each employee, adjusted for the percentage of time spent by that employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities). Additionally, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Québec nexus ratio for the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) is calculated using R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (unreduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold, and excluding pre-commercialization expenditures). Claimants file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (along with Form RD-222-V, Form RD-1029.8.PR-T, and Form RD-1029.8.EN-T) with their CO-17 return within 12 months after the CO-17 filing deadline.
B. Legacy Québec Regime (Taxation Years Beginning Before March 26, 2025)

Corporations and individuals whose taxation year (or partnership fiscal period) began before March 26, 2025, claim the legacy R&D tax credits (Form RD-1029.7-V and Form RD-222-V), which provide a 30% refundable rate for corporations with prior-year assets under $50,000,000 (phasing down to 14% between $50,000,000 and $75,000,000 in assets) and a 14% basic refundable rate, subject to the $50,000 base exclusion threshold.
4.3 Western, Atlantic, and Northern Provincial/Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (BC)) provides a 10% refundable credit to CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations on up to $6,000,000 of qualified BC expenditures for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (maximum $600,000 refund, with the expenditure limit phasing out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital, as amended following BC Budget 2026, which also made the credit permanent) and a 10% non-refundable credit for other corporations and excess expenditures (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years), claimed on Form T666 (or Schedule 425 for partnership allocations after April 14, 2026) within 18 months of tax year-end. In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act) is a fully refundable grant on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D spending (phasing out over $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital), providing an 8% base payment on spending up to the corporation's base level (average spending over the previous 2 years) and an enhanced 20% payment on incremental spending above the base level, claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the AT1 filing due date.

In Saskatchewan, the R&D tax credit (sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan)) provides CCPCs with a 10% refundable credit up to $1,000,000 in expenditures and a 10% non-refundable credit on excess expenditures and for non-CCPCs (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years), claimed on Schedule T2SCH403. In Manitoba, the R&D tax credit (section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba)) is 15% on eligible Manitoba expenditures, of which one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable for in-house R&D (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years), or 100% refundable (15%) for R&D under contract with a qualifying Manitoba institute, claimed on Schedule T2SCH380 within 1 year after the T2 filing due date.

All three participating Atlantic provinces provide a flat 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap: Nova Scotia (section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), claimed on Schedule T2SCH340 within 18 months of year-end, with an option to renounce within 6 months of year-end), New Brunswick (section 59 of the New Brunswick Income Tax Act, claimed on Schedule T2SCH360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (section 42 of the Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador), claimed on Schedule T2SCH301 for corporations or Form T1129 for individuals within 12 months after the filing due date). Finally, the Yukon provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.
