body.text: 4.5 Federal-Provincial Stacking Mechanics and Mathematical Walkthrough (Proxy Method)

Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, they reduce the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(18) in the year earned (unless formally renounced by the income tax return filing due date). Under the Proxy Method, the CRA’s Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy and Assistance and Contract Payments Policy establish a dual accounting treatment for provincial credits. First, the entire provincial R&D tax credit (both the portion earned on direct expenditures and the portion earned on the notional 55% PPA) reduces Section 127 federal qualified expenditures on Lines 513–514 of Form T661 regardless of whether the provincial credit is refundable or non-refundable. Second, because the notional PPA is not included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, the portion of the provincial tax credit relating to the PPA does not reduce the Section 37 pool on Line 429; instead, that PPA-related portion of the provincial credit must be included directly in net income for tax purposes on Schedule T2SCH1 in the year received under paragraph 12(1)(x) of the ITA.

To illustrate this interaction, consider a Qualifying CCPC in Ontario (with prior-year taxable capital under $15,000,000 and prior-year taxable income under $500,000) that incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee SR&ED salaries in Ontario during its 2026 taxation year and elects the Proxy Method:

items: Direct Section 37 Pool Addition: $1,000,000 (Line 300 and Line 400).
Notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (55% PPA): $1,000,000 × 55% = $550,000 (Line 502).
Gross Qualified Expenditures Before Provincial Assistance: $1,000,000 + $550,000 = $1,550,000.

Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC at 8% Refundable): $1,550,000 × 8% = $124,000. Of this $124,000 OITC, $80,000 ($1,000,000 × 8%) relates to direct salaries and reduces the Section 37 pool on Line 429, while $44,000 ($550,000 × 8%) relates to the notional PPA and is included in income on Schedule T2SCH1 when received under paragraph 12(1)(x).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC at 3.5% Non-Refundable): Calculated on Ontario qualified expenditures reduced by the OITC: ($1,550,000 − $124,000) × 3.5% = $1,426,000 × 3.5% = $49,910.

Federal Enhanced ITC (35% Refundable) Net of Ontario Assistance: Subtracting both the $124,000 OITC and $49,910 ORDTC from the $1,550,000 gross qualified pool leaves $1,376,090 in federal qualified expenditures on Line 570. Applying the 35% enhanced refundable rate yields $481,631.50 in federal cash refunds ($1,376,090 × 35%), resulting in $655,541.50 in total combined federal and Ontario tax credits (65.55% of the $1,000,000 cash payroll outlay), of which $605,631.50 is an immediate cash refund. (Alternatively, if the corporation is in a loss position and renounces the non-refundable $49,910 ORDTC by its filing due date, its federal qualified expenditure pool remains $1,426,000, generating $499,100 in refundable federal ITCs and $623,100 in total combined federal and OITC cash refunds.)

body.text: 5. Governing Bodies, Prescribed Forms, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Deadlines, and Audit Review Procedures
5.1 Division of Institutional Authority

In Canada’s federal governance framework, authority over the SR&ED program is divided between two federal institutions. The Department of Finance Canada formulates tax policy, drafts legislative amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (such as Bill C-15 and the Budget 2026 proposals), and approves prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the program nationwide through its Business Tax Incentives Directorate in Ottawa and regional SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs). Within the CRA, scientific and technological eligibility is evaluated by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) reporting to Research and Technology Managers (RTMs), while expenditure compliance and ITC calculations are audited by Financial Reviewers (FRs) reporting to Financial Review Managers (FRMs).
5.2 Complete Architecture of Modernized Form T661 (May 2026 Revision) and Companion Schedules

To access SR&ED deductions and ITCs, a claimant must submit prescribed Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 2026) along with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit — Corporations, updated May 22, 2026) for corporations, or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit — Individuals) for individuals and trusts. (Note that for "classified projects" designated by a federal agency for national security, Part 2 Section B project descriptions must be submitted on a separate sheet mailed directly to the CRA Business Tax Incentives Directorate in Ottawa.)
Modernized Form T661 is organized into ten parts:

items: Part 1 — General Information (Lines 010 to 162): Captures the claimant's name (Line 010), total number of projects claimed (Line 050), contact details (Lines 100–125), partnership information (Lines 151–157), and the election to use the Proxy Method (Line 160) or Traditional Method (Line 162).

Part 2 — Project Data and Technical Narrative (Lines 200 to 282): Requires the project title (Line 200), start and completion dates (Lines 202–204), mandatory Canada Research and Development Classification (CRDC) field-of-science or technology code (Line 206), Pre-Claim Approval indicator (Line 212) and assigned Pre-Claim Approval Case Number (Line 214), and the three core technical narrative sections: Line 242 (technological obstacles or uncertainties encountered), Line 244 (work performed in the tax year to overcome those obstacles), and Line 246 (scientific or technological advancements achieved). Lines 253–261 record key internal and external personnel and qualifications. For post-December 15, 2024 capital claims, Line 262 requires the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024, used in the project (claimed on Line 390), and Line 263 requires the percentage of total operating time for each listed property. Lines 270–282 record contemporaneous project planning and supporting documentation.

Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures and Section 37 Pool (Lines 300 to 470): Captures domestic wages for non-specified employees (Line 300) and specified employees (Line 305), foreign wages up to the 10% cap for non-specified (Line 307) and specified (Line 309) employees, prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310), current-year wages unpaid after 180 days (Line 315), materials consumed (Line 320) and transformed (Line 325), arm's-length contracts (Line 340) and non-arm's length contracts (Line 345), Traditional Method overhead and equipment leases (Line 360), third-party payments (Line 370), total current expenditures (Line 380), restored ASA capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 (Line 390), and total allowable expenditures (Line 400). Lines 429–470 adjust for provincial, other government, and non-government assistance (Lines 429–432), sale/CCA recapture of SR&ED capital assets (Line 440), prior-year pool balances (Line 450), current deductions claimed, and closing Section 37 pool carryforwards (Line 470).

Part 4 — Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 500 to 570): Incorporates the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504 — 25% First-Term and 25% Second-Term), qualified expenditures transferred from a NAL performer via Form T1146 (Line 508), provincial/other government/non-government assistance and contract payments (Lines 513–517), unpaid non-salary current expenses at 180 days (Line 520), payments to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), prescribed capital and transfer adjustments for post-December 15, 2024 property (Lines 532, 535, 540), and Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570).

Part 5 — Prescribed Proxy Amount (Lines 810 to 820 & Boxes 850 to 860): Computes the non-specified employee salary base net of bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits (Lines 810–814), the specified employee proxy salary base capped at the lesser of 75% of base salary and 2.5 × YMPE (Boxes 850–860 and Line 816), the total Salary Base (Line 818), and the 55% PPA (Line 820, subject to the overall cap).

Part 6 — Project Costs and Shared-Use Equipment Breakdown: Details project-level cost allocations and lists the 20 most expensive Shared-Use Equipment properties acquired after December 15, 2024 (including Box 792 for 25% of the capital cost).

Part 9 — Claim Preparer Information (Lines 935 to 975) and the $1,000 Penalty (ITA s. 162(5.1)–(5.3)): Requires disclosure of whether an external claim preparer accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim (Line 935), along with each preparer’s name (Line 940), 15-character Business Number (Line 945), billing arrangement code (Line 950: Code 1 for contingency fee, Code 2 for hourly rate, Code 4 for flat fee), billing rate (Line 955), and total fee paid or payable (Line 965). Under subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the ITA, missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 information triggers a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable.
Part 10 — Certification (Lines 165 to 175): Signed and dated by an authorized signing officer.

body.text: 5.3 The Elective CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process introduced in Budget 2025 to provide businesses with upfront technical eligibility certainty before starting work or incurring R&D costs. Pre-claim approval is open to CCPCs, Canadian corporations, and Canadian partnerships that have an annual gross income of less than $25,000,000, are in good compliance standing with the CRA, and submit proposed future projects (up to three projects per application) that have not been previously claimed or litigated.
The application follows a four-step workflow:

items: Step 1 — Open a Pre-Claim Approval Request: Complete the online web form (under 5 minutes) to receive a case number within 2 to 5 business days.
Step 2 — Apply in My Business Account: Submit Form T1322 in My Business Account using existing project documentation for up to three projects.
Step 3 — Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist: Held within 4 weeks of submitting the application (mandatory for new SR&ED claimants; optional as needed for returning claimants in good standing).
Step 4 — Receive Official Determination: Issued by the CRA within 8 weeks of completing the application in My Business Account.

body.text: If granted, pre-claim approval is valid for up to three years. While the claimant must still file Form T661 annually (reporting the case number on Line 214) to substantiate expenditures, refundable claims containing only pre-approved projects that require an expenditure review have their processing service standard cut in half—from 180 days down to 90 days.
5.4 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Absolute Bar of Subsection 220(2.2)

Under subsection 37(11) (for the expenditure pool) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for the ITC), a taxpayer’s SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the filing due date of the income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a taxable corporation’s T2 return is due 6 months after its taxation year-end under paragraph 150(1)(a), the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, June 30, 2026, for a December 31, 2024 year-end). For unincorporated individuals (June 15 T1 filing due date), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the end of the tax year. For trusts (T3 due 90 days after year-end under paragraph 150(1)(c)), the reporting deadline is 15 months after the trust's year-end. For tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j), Form T661 is due on the return filing due date (6 months after year-end) under subsection 149(7).

Under subsection 37(11.1) and subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, the SR&ED reporting deadline is absolute. Subsection 220(2.2) prohibits the Minister from exercising discretion under subsection 220(2.1) to waive or extend the filing deadline for prescribed SR&ED forms or prescribed information, and Taxpayer Relief provisions under subsection 220(3.1) apply only to penalties and interest. Any SR&ED expenditure or ITC not reported on prescribed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) by the reporting deadline (extended only to the next business day if the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognised public holiday) is permanently lost. Only the deduction of an existing Section 37 pool balance and Part 9 claim preparer disclosures are exempt from the reporting deadline.
5.5 CRA Service Standards, Audit Review Workflow, Escalation Hierarchy, and Gross Negligence Penalties

For refundable SR&ED claims, the CRA’s processing service standards are 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed without review, 90 calendar days for claims selected for review where all projects received Pre-Claim Approval, and 180 calendar days for claims selected for review that include any unapproved project (or any project that materially diverged from its pre-claim approval). First-time claimants or claimants who have not filed in the past 3 years may be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS).

Once a claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 is part of the certified tax return. Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April/July 2026) and the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, the assigned RTA and FR contact the claimant by phone and send an initial letter with a meeting agenda and a 30-day timeline for pre-meeting information requests. Most review meetings and facility tours are conducted virtually via videoconferencing (with on-site visits granted on an exceptional basis). RTAs are prohibited from negotiating eligibility or expenditure amounts, must archive critical evidence for adverse decisions in the TF98 file, and must consult their Research and Technology Manager (RTM) before disallowing a claim for lack of information, issuing an unfavourable decision without a site visit, issuing a formal "Better Books and Records" letter, or proposing penalties. Under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the ITA, claimants must retain all supporting technical and financial records for 6 years from the end of the taxation year. If adjustments are proposed, the CRA issues a Proposal Package (containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and financial proposal letter), giving the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations.
Under the CRA’s Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (updated December 5, 2025), claimants follow a four-step dispute resolution hierarchy:

items: Step 1 — Talk to the RTA and/or FR: Resolve factual misunderstandings directly with the reviewers.
Step 2 — Contact the RTM and/or FRM: Escalate unresolved issues to the reviewers' managers.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532): Before the file is closed and before the 30-day proposal period expires, submit Form RC532 to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5). Assigned within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the review evaluates whether the claimant received due process and whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, resulting in a Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection and Tax Court Appeal: File a Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment (with further right of appeal to the Tax Court of Canada). (Federal Budget 2026 proposed extending the objection period for individuals and graduated rate estates to the later of one year from assessment mailing and two years after the return filing due date, effective three months after Royal Assent.)

body.text: Finally, under subsection 163(2) of the ITA (and the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy, updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim, the penalty is the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of: (a) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement (paragraph 163(2)(a), where taxable income is deemed not less than zero under subsection 163(2.1) for loss corporations deducting non-business or false expenses), plus (b) the entire overstated refundable ITC refund claimed (paragraph 163(2)(d)). Under subsection 163(3), the CRA bears the burden of proof to establish knowing misrepresentation or gross negligence.
6. Judicial Precedents, Audit Case Law, and the Evolution of Eligibility Doctrine

Although the CRA replaced its 2012/2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy on August 13, 2021, with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives—which frame eligibility around The "Why" Requirement (advancing scientific knowledge or achieving technological advancement by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty) and The "How" Requirement (conducting a systematic investigation or search by formulating a hypothesis, testing it via experiment or analysis, developing logical conclusions, and keeping contemporaneous evidence)—the Federal Court of Appeal has held that CRA administrative guidelines are not binding on the courts. Courts adjudicating SR&ED appeals apply the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act through binding judicial precedent.
6.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies

The foundational precedent governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is Judge Donald Bowman’s decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC). Building on Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC) (which established that "systematic investigation" excludes routine engineering and unsystematic trial-and-error), Judge Bowman articulated five criteria that were approved by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] FCJ No. 1890 (FCA), and summarized as five mandatory affirmative questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 284 N.R. 386:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? ("Routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field.)
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?

Did the process result in a technological advancement? (This includes an advancement in general understanding recognizable to experts in the field, including the conclusive rejection of an unsuccessful hypothesis.)
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?

RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] FCJ No. 1890
Repeatability of testing & role of documentary vs. oral evidence

Approved Northwest Hydraulic; held that scientific testing requires repeatability of testing data, and clarified that while written contemporaneous records are the strongest evidence, written documents are not an absolute statutory precondition if credible oral or other evidence proves systematic testing.
116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] ACI No. 478 (QL)
Absence of written test reports vs. witness credibility

Justice Archambault held that while lacking contemporaneous written reports places a taxpayer in a "very precarious position", the Act does not require written reports; oral testimony can establish SR&ED if witness credibility is high.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 284 N.R. 386
Formally summarized Judge Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic criteria into the five mandatory affirmative questions applied in all subsequent SR&ED appeals.
Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597
Emphasized that contemporaneous documentation of the claimed work is important as the best evidence of systematic investigation.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355
Addressed the delineation of experimental production and materials transformed under the SR&ED provisions.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313; 6379249 Canada Inc., 2015 TCC 77; R&D Pro-Innovation Inc., 2015 TCC 186
Independence of CRA RTAs as expert witnesses & non-binding nature of CRA policy

Justice Jorré ruled that CRA RTAs testifying as experts must provide independent expert opinions rather than relying on CRA guidelines, and reiterated that contemporaneous documents with specific content are not a condition imposed by the Act.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6

Justice Sommerfeldt reviewed jurisprudence on "routine engineering" (para. 17) and defined a "hypothesis" (para. 26) as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" specifically aimed at reducing technological uncertainty.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, 2021 DTC 5050
Mandatory legal nature of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria
Affirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the proper judicial interpretation of the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1).
National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)
"Engineering method" vs. "scientific method", CRA 2021 guidelines & expert witness admissibility

Landmark appellate ruling affirming that (1) the Northwest Hydraulic scientific method test is mandatory; (2) CRA's 2021 "Why/How" guidelines do not bind courts or reject Northwest Hydraulic; and (3) an expert report 65% written by the taxpayer is inadmissible under White Burgess and Tax Court Rule 145.
Objective knowledge gap & sufficiency of oral + log evidence in food science

Chief Justice Rossiter held that lacking knowledge must exist in the scientific/technological knowledge base (not simply be unknown to the claimant), and allowed frozen pie formulation claims where structured recipe hypotheses, failure analyses, and credible CEO testimony satisfied the five questions.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (TCC, 2025)
Shelf-stability formulation uncertainty & application of the Five Questions

Applied Northwest Hydraulic, C.W. Agencies, Joel Theatrical, and Canafric to hold that developing a canned, shelf-stable cold-pressed juice drink faced genuine technological uncertainty not resolvable by routine engineering, allowing the taxpayer's 2020 SR&ED claim.

body.text: 6.3 Deep-Dive Legal Analysis of Recent Appellate and Trial Jurisprudence
1. National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)

In National R&D Inc., the appellant taxpayer appealed a Tax Court of Canada judgment (2020 TCC 47, per Justice Lafleur) that had found the existence of technological risk or uncertainty (Question 1) but dismissed the SR&ED claim because the taxpayer failed Questions 2 through 5. Before the Federal Court of Appeal (Rennie, Woods, and Laskin JJ.A.), the taxpayer argued that: (a) the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are mere guidance rather than mandatory prerequisites, that the "scientific method" is not explicitly mentioned in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, and that the engineering method differs from the scientific method; (b) the CRA’s revised August 13, 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives had rejected the Northwest Hydraulic criteria; and (c) the Tax Court judge erred in excluding the taxpayer's expert witness report.

Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal dismissing the appeal with costs, Justice Rennie rejected every ground of appeal. Citing Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada (2005 SCC 54), the Court reaffirmed that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are not ultra vires statutory provisions, but represent the binding judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) enacted by Parliament. The Court noted that revised CRA guidance still requires underlying rigour and discipline, and emphasized that CRA administrative policy guidance is not binding on the courts. Moreover, the Court held that whether a material distinction exists between the scientific method and the engineering method in applied versus natural sciences is a question of fact that must be proven through qualified expert testimony subject to cross-examination, rather than by attaching academic literature to a book of authorities. On the evidentiary record, National R&D did not conduct its work methodically, kept vague and conclusory records, and failed to show how hypotheses were modified following testing. Finally, applying White Burgess Langille Inman v. Abbott and Haliburton Co. (2015 SCC 23) and section 145(2) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure), the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the exclusion of the taxpayer’s expert witness report because the taxpayer had written 65% of the expert's report (destroying independence and impartiality and turning the report into advocacy) and because the report improperly offered an opinion on the domestic legal question of whether the facts satisfied the statutory test.
2. Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King

Conversely, the Tax Court of Canada’s decisions in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King illustrate how taxpayers can successfully overturn CRA audit disallowances when they present credible factual evidence demonstrating a systematic investigation. In Canafric (para. 89), then Chief Justice Rossiter stated the foundational rule that "the lacking knowledge must exist in the base of scientific or technological knowledge, not simply be unknown to the claimant". In that case, Canafric—a manufacturer of custom frozen pies for retailers—had $343,449 in SR&ED expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs disallowed by the CRA across its 2013–2016 taxation years. The Tax Court found that Canafric faced genuine technological uncertainties because no publicly available food-science knowledge explained how to simultaneously achieve a 21-day shelf life without preservatives, reduced salt and fat, higher protein, shorter cooking times, and structural pie integrity after freezing.

In both Canafric and Manning Canning (which involved developing a canned, shelf-stable drink containing cold-pressed juice in the 2020 taxation year), the CRA argued that the taxpayers merely engaged in routine "trial and error". Rejecting the CRA’s characterization, the Tax Court held that formulating specific causal hypotheses aimed at overcoming the uncertainty (per Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6), testing recipes, analyzing why unsuccessful formulations failed, and systematically modifying the recipes based on those results satisfied the scientific method under Questions 2 and 3. Furthermore, the Court reaffirmed that technological advancement (Question 4) includes failed trials that eliminate non-viable hypotheses and advance general understanding, and held under Question 5 (citing RIS-Christie, 99 DTC 5087) that detailed, credible oral testimony from the taxpayer's CEO can bridge gaps in documentary records to establish SR&ED eligibility on a balance of probabilities.
